title: When Systematic Phonics Instruction Wasn't Enough
author: Knowledge Exchange
summary: A second-grade teacher describes her multi-year journey tutoring one persistently struggling reader through three sequential, targeted interventions after standard phonics instruction proved insufficient. When the student entered second grade reading just 19 words per minute at 86% accuracy, she began with Reading Mastery Signature Edition, which atomized decoding into discrete skills practiced to mastery through spaced retrieval, producing confidence gains alongside foundational skill development. Over the summer and into third grade she introduced EBLI (Evidence Based Literacy Instruction), a sounds-first, curriculum-agnostic approach that unlocked multisyllabic word reading and brought accuracy to 92%. When fluency plateaued at around 53 words per minute despite accuracy gains, she added Precision Teaching using a Standard Celeration Chart with daily timed readings and explicit goal-setting, which broke the plateau and brought the student to 76 words correct at 94% accuracy by year's end. The article's central argument is that no single intervention is sufficient for the most resistant readers, and that combining programs in sequence -- each targeting a distinct sub-skill deficit -- is more powerful than any one approach alone. The key clinical insight is that plateau at one level is diagnostic: it signals the need to add or switch the intervention targeting the next deficit in the skill hierarchy.
points: Reading Mastery's highly interactive, discrete-skills, spaced-retrieval structure was critical for a student with fragile confidence -- it provided a high success rate while rebuilding foundational decoding from scratch.

EBLI's sounds-first, curriculum-agnostic approach unlocked multisyllabic word reading through split-word strategies, moving the student from paralysis in the face of unknown words to independent decoding on grade-level text.

Precision Teaching's Standard Celeration Chart provided daily concrete goal-setting and visible progress tracking, breaking a three-month fluency plateau by compressing feedback loops to a daily cycle.

The case demonstrates that different interventions target distinct reading sub-skills (decoding, accuracy, fluency) -- plateau at one level is a diagnostic signal to address the next deficit, not to persist with the same approach.

All three programs are valuable alone, but their combination is more powerful: Reading Mastery builds the skill base, EBLI generalizes it to connected text, and Precision Teaching builds the automaticity needed for fluency.
quotes: Six of those students ended the year proficient or advanced on the end of year assessments. Reading Mastery gave them the skills to master decoding and accelerate into grade level text.

Reading Mastery was ideal for this because reading instruction is atomized into discreet skills and practiced to mastery through highly interactive student application and immediate feedback. Skills are also interleaved and practiced systematically through spaced retrieval.

EBLI is a sounds-first approach that encompasses all aspects of literacy. It is also curriculum agnostic, giving me the flexibility to apply the strategies to any text. It also introduces students to grade level (and above) vocabulary and text, accelerating their growth.

The EBLI multisyllabic split-word reading and spelling strategies helped my student recognize common spelling patterns that developed his accuracy when reading multisyllabic words. The EBLI oral reading practice strategies helped him develop his accuracy and fluency when reading grade level text.

The daily goal setting gave him a concrete goal that showed him what he was aiming for and feedback that motivated him to improve. Seeing his daily success and growth toward his goal empowered him to keep improving.

My biggest takeaway: If something isn't working, don't be afraid to bring in something new. All three resources -- Reading Mastery, EBLI, and Precision Teaching -- are valuable on their own, but combined, they are very powerful in helping a student become a successful reader.

I see a child that came to me barely able to decode, paralyzed by an unknown word, with no skills to break down the word, and minimal confidence in his reading ability, transformed into a confident reader. He is reading grade level chapter books and vocabulary. He's reading out loud in class. He's happy and proud.
